title: A. Setup
text: This setup guide will help you install the necessary tools and dependencies to follow and run this workshop code on your local machine unless you are using a cloud-based environment. The workshop code is designed to run in a Linux environment, so if you are using Windows, we recommend installing Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL2). If you are using macOS or Linux, you can skip the WSL installation and use your native terminal.

title: A. Setup
text:
1. Install WSL2 and Ubuntu

Open the Windows Start menu, search for PowerShell, and choose Run as administrator.
Run the following command in Windows PowerShell:

wsl --install -d Ubuntu

Restart Windows if prompted.
Launch Ubuntu from the Start menu and wait for first-time initialization.
Create your Ubuntu username and password when prompted. Password characters are not displayed while typing.

Check installation in Windows PowerShell:
wsl --list --verbose
You should see Ubuntu with VERSION equal to 2. If Ubuntu is version 1, use:
wsl --set-version Ubuntu 2
If wsl --install displays help instead of installing, try wsl --list --online, then wsl --install -d Ubuntu. If installation is blocked by policy or virtualization, contact your IT administrator. Do not attempt to bypass institutional restrictions.
Official guide: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/install

title: A. Setup
text:
2. Install Visual Studio Code
If you do not have VS Code installed, follow these steps:

Download VS Code for Windows: https://code.visualstudio.com/download.
Install VS Code on Windows (not inside Ubuntu).
Open VS Code → Extensions (Ctrl+Shift+X). Install:

3. Get the repository
On Windows, open WSL2, On Linux or macOS, use a terminal and install Git, wget, CDO and Python 3.11+ using your operating system’s package manager,
Then run:
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y git wget curl ca-certificates cdo python3 python3-venv python3-pip
Keep the project inside the Linux filesystem on WSL | in your home directory (for Linux and macOS), for example:
mkdir -p ~/projects
cd ~/projects
git clone https://github.com/khizerzakir/tutorial-repo.git
cd tutorial-repo
Open the repository from Ubuntu/terminal with the command code dot.

4. Check your tools
cdo -V

wget --version | head -n 1
If you use uv, also run uv –version. If CDO is missing, install it through your OS package manager or a conda-forge environment; CDO is not installed by uv or pip.

title: A. Setup
text:
5. Install Python dependencies
The Zarr builder in this repository requires Zarr 3; use Python 3.12 or newer.

Option A: uv
Install uv using the official instructions, then from the repository root run:
uv sync --locked
Check the core packages and Zarr major version:
uv run python -c "import xarray, zarr; print(xarray.__version__, zarr.__version__)"


Option B: pip
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python -c "import xarray, zarr; print(xarray.__version__, zarr.__version__)"
Confirm that the printed Zarr version is 3 or newer before running the cube builder. If the environment resolves Zarr 2, use Python 3.12+ and reinstall the project dependencies.

Important: Keep the virtual environment activated for subsequent terminal commands. When you open a new Ubuntu terminal, run source .venv/bin/activate again. Do not use sudo pip install. The requirements.txt must be committed to github and kept consistent with the tested uv.lock; pip does not read uv.lock automatically.

title: C. Build and inspect a Zarr cube
text:
1. Check the interim files
The builder expects NetCDF files under data/interim/ and dimensions named time, lat and lon.
find data/interim -name '*_processed.nc' -type f
cdo -s sinfo data/interim/METREF/2020/06/example_processed.nc
Replace the example filename with one of your actual outputs. Confirm time and coordinate dimensions and inspect valid values before building the cube. If your files use x and y, update the dimension names and chunk configuration in code/build_zarr_cube.py.
crumbs: C. Build and inspect a Zarr cube

title: C. Build and inspect a Zarr cube
text:
2. Build the cube
From the repository root:
uv run python code/03_build_zarr_cube.py
The script uses xarray to open multiple files by coordinates and Dask for lazy/chunked processing. It writes to:
data/zarr/example.zarr/
The current builder requires Zarr 3. Use a Python environment that resolves Zarr 3 as required by the script. The script removes an existing output store before rebuilding; copy or rename any output you need to keep first.

title: C. Build and inspect a Zarr cube
text:
3. Understand chunks, shards and compression
The script currently starts with:
INNER_CHUNKS = {"time": 1, "lat": 256, "lon": 256}
SHARD_CHUNKS = {"time": 10, "lat": 512, "lon": 512}
COMPRESSOR = BloscCodec(cname="zstd", clevel=5, shuffle="shuffle")








Setting
Role
Trade-off




Inner chunks
Small independently readable blocks
Smaller blocks help selective reads but add metadata/overhead


Shards
Group storage for multiple inner chunks
Larger shards reduce object count but may make writes/updates coarser


Zstd compression
Reduces stored bytes
Higher compression can use more CPU



These are initial values, not universal optima. Benchmark common access patterns: a map at one time, a point/area time series, and a small regional subset.

title: C. Build and inspect a Zarr cube
text:
6. Scaling beyond the sample
For a priority subset, measure runtime, peak memory, interim and Zarr sizes, valid coverage and read speed. Expand to a larger region or a 2,000 km corridor by processing grid-aligned spatial tiles and time batches. Add a remapping margin at tile boundaries, then remove duplicate edge cells from the final grid.
Parallelize independent NetCDF files or tiles up to the measured CPU, memory, storage and network limits of the available workstation/VM. Use isolated temporary stores or non-overlapping Zarr regions; avoid concurrent writes to the same chunk/shard. Keep a manifest and rerun only failed batches. Re-benchmark chunks and shards on the larger workload.

Troubleshooting







Symptom
Checks




No interim files
Check downloader output, input path and CDO log


Many NaNs after remapping
Compare raw AOI, crop bounds and target-grid bounds; inspect fill values and source QA


Zarr dimension error
Print ds.sizes; rename coordinates or change chunk dimensions


Zarr version error
Check uv run python -c “import zarr; print(zarr.__version__)“; script needs version 3 or newer


Slow writes or reads
Check RAM/disk I/O, chunk and shard sizes, and number of parallel tasks


Output already exists
Builder replaces its output; back up the store or change OUTPUT in the script

Study period: 2013–2015 · Spatial unit: matched origin/destination zones · Time unit: half-month







Data
Zone × period summary




METREF
Half-month cumulative ETo and mean daily ETo


FVC
Half-month mean FVC and change from the previous period


Mobility
Departures, returns or migrants; counts and population-adjusted rates



Maps: climate and mobility side by side; then map co-occurrence classes such as high ETo + low FVC + high departures.

APIs, cloud platforms and this workflow
APIs, Microsoft Planetary Computer and Google Earth Engine are useful for discovering, accessing and analyzing many datasets.
This tutorial demonstrates a local, explicit path for selected authenticated LSA SAF data when we need to document a regional crop, target grid and processing choices. The two approaches can complement each other; this workflow does not assume hosted platforms lack the required data.

Step 1 · Download a small sample
cp code/.env.example code/.env   # add credentials; keep local
bash code/01_download_sample.sh 2020 06

The downloader reads a product URL, year and month from settings.
Raw files go under data/raw/YYYY/MM/.
It downloads to a temporary .part file, then renames on success.

Start with one month and one product. It makes troubleshooting and validation manageable.

section: Download · safe, parallel, with a time estimate
text:
Download · safe, parallel, with a time estimate
get() { local f="$2/${1##*/}"
        wget -q -O "$f.part" "$1" && mv "$f.part" "$f"; }
t0=$SECONDS; get "$(head -n1 <<< "$pending")" "$DEST"
tail -n +2 <<< "$pending" \
  | xargs -P "$JOBS" -I{} bash -c 'get "$1" "$2"' _ {} "$DEST"

A file only gets its final name when the download is complete; interrupted runs never leave half-files that look finished.
Timing the first file gives an estimate for the rest; JOBS sets parallel downloads.

Resampling is a decision








Method
Typical use
Main trade-off




Bilinear
Continuous fields such as many climate variables
Smooths values; can modify extremes


Nearest neighbour
Categories and QA flags
Preserves classes; can look blocky



Neither method creates finer source detail. For each product, choose a method that matches its values and intended use; retain and apply quality flags where available.

from zarr.codecs import BloscCodec
INNER_CHUNKS = {"time": 1, "lat": 256, "lon": 256}

Inner chunks are the read units: one date and a spatial window.
Shards group chunks to reduce the number of storage objects.

title: Climate Data Cubes
text:
Caveats and uncertainty

Missing values may be real masks/quality exclusions or processing/configuration problems.
A crop/grid mismatch, wrong variable, coordinate issue or fill-value handling can cause extensive NaNs.
Bilinear remapping smooths; nearest-neighbour can be blocky. Different choices can change statistics.
Degree grids have latitude-dependent ground dimensions.
Product versions, temporal support, units and quality systems may differ.
The example is a regional teaching workflow, not a validated operational climate product.

section: On-the-fly processing vs a pre-built cube
text:
On-the-fly processing vs a pre-built cube









On-the-fly (catalog + lazy loading)
Pre-built cube (this tutorial)




Regridding / resampling
Done at read time; settings are easy to overlook
Fixed once and documented in the pipeline


Compute cost
Paid at every query
Paid once, up front


Storage
Reuses the provider’s data
Creates a derived copy


Changing area, grid or method
Change the query
Re-run the pipeline


Following provider updates
Automatic
Needs a rebuild



Neither is better in general. Choose by use case, and always record the resampling choice.

title: Climate Data Cubes
text:
Scale the pilot carefully
For a large domain (for example, a 2,000 km corridor), first benchmark a representative priority subset:

Record runtime, peak memory, file size, valid coverage and output read speed.
Split work into grid-aligned spatial tiles and/or time batches.
Parallelize independent files within measured CPU, memory and I/O limits.
Add remapping margins at tile edges and trim duplicate target cells.
Write non-overlapping Zarr regions or isolated stores; track and retry failures.

Do not scale only by multiplying worker count. Disk throughput, memory, output object counts and safe Zarr writes can become the bottleneck.

title: Climate Data Cubes
text:
Possible next updates

Harmonize clip and target-grid bounds; add a coverage map and threshold.
Apply product-specific quality flags and test decoded no-data values.
Record provenance, product versions, units, grid and resampling settings.
Benchmark chunk/shard sizes for intended queries and available compute/storage.
Add more products only after documenting their spatial and temporal semantics.
Add automated tests for sample input files and failed/partial outputs.

from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import xarray as xr

def find_repo_root() -> Path:
    for candidate in [Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents]:
        if (candidate / "data").is_dir():
            return candidate
    raise FileNotFoundError("Could not find a repository containing data/")

def compute_scalar(value):
    value = value.compute() if hasattr(value, "compute") else value
    return value.item() if hasattr(value, "item") else value

def inspect_store(kind: str, path: Path) -> list[dict]:
    relative_path = path.relative_to(REPO_ROOT)
    print(f"\n{kind.upper()}: {relative_path}")
    opener = xr.open_zarr(path, consolidated=False) if kind == "zarr" else xr.open_dataset(path, decode_cf=True, mask_and_scale=True)
    with opener as ds:
        print("Dimensions:", dict(ds.sizes))
        print("Coordinates:", list(ds.coords))
        print("Data variables:", list(ds.data_vars))
        print("Global attributes:", dict(ds.attrs))
        print("Dataset encoding keys:", sorted(ds.encoding))
        rows = []
        for name, da in ds.variables.items():
            size = int(da.size)
            missing = int(compute_scalar(da.isnull().sum())) if size else 0
            row = {"store_type": kind, "path": str(relative_path), "name": name,
                   "role": "coordinate" if name in ds.coords else "data",
                   "dtype": str(da.dtype), "dims": tuple(da.dims), "shape": tuple(da.shape),
                   "size": size, "missing": missing,
                   "missing_pct": round(100 * missing / size, 3) if size else 0.0,
                   "attrs": dict(da.attrs)}
            if size and da.dtype.kind in "iufc":
                row["finite"] = int(compute_scalar(np.isfinite(da).sum()))
                if row["finite"]:
                    row["min"] = compute_scalar(da.min(skipna=True))
                    row["max"] = compute_scalar(da.max(skipna=True))
            rows.append(row)
            print(f"  {name}: missing={missing}/{size} ({row['missing_pct']}%), dtype={row['dtype']}, shape={row['shape']}")
        return rows

REPO_ROOT = find_repo_root()

title: Adaptive cube plotting
text:
adaptive_cube_plot.py provides importable plotting functions for xarray cubes:

plot_time_slices: time-index/date panel maps with shared colour scale, Cartopy projection, inferred data extent, coastlines/borders and optional GeoDataFrame boundaries.
plot_spatial_timeseries: time series at selected points and area summaries.
plot_climate_mobility_period: side-by-side climate and aggregated origin/destination mobility maps for a selected half-month.



Install the project dependencies plus optional geospatial packages:
pip install matplotlib numpy pandas xarray cartopy geopandas pyarrow pyproj
Cartopy may need system libraries depending on the platform. Importing the module and using time-series plotting does not require Cartopy; map functions do.



From the repository root:
from code.plot_utils.adaptive_cube_plot import (
    plot_time_slices,
    plot_spatial_timeseries,
    plot_climate_mobility_period,
)
If code is not a Python package in the local checkout, add its parent directory to sys.path, or add code/plot_utils directly:
import sys
from pathlib import Path
sys.path.insert(0, str(Path.cwd() / "code" / "plot_utils"))
from adaptive_cube_plot import plot_time_slices



import xarray as xr
from adaptive_cube_plot import plot_time_slices

ds = xr.open_zarr("data/zarr/metref_sample_1month.zarr")
fig, axes = plot_time_slices(
    ds,
    var="METREF",
    time_index=[0, 5, 10],
    data_crs="EPSG:4326",
    ncols=3,
    show=False,
)
The map extent is calculated from the selected coordinates. Set extent=(xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax) to crop all panels to a common area. data_crs describes the existing coordinate values; it does not reproject the data. Longitude/latitude coordinate names imply EPSG:4326. For projected x/y, pass the actual CRS (for example, data_crs="EPSG:32628"). Regional geographic maps default to a local Lambert Conformal projection to avoid the visual x-axis stretch of plotting longitude and latitude as equal Cartesian units. Pass a Cartopy CRS as map_crs to override it.
Overlay an AOI or administrative boundary:
import geopandas as gpd
boundaries = gpd.read_file("data/aoi.geojson")
fig, axes = plot_time_slices(
    ds, var="METREF", time_index=[0, 5], data_crs="EPSG:4326",
    boundaries=boundaries, ncols=2, show=False,
)
If a boundary file has no embedded CRS, provide boundary_crs. This assigns the source CRS metadata. Confirm the source CRS before assigning it.



The mobility table is expected to contain an origin or destination ID, a date/period column, and a numeric metric. Defaults match the normalized OD schema (norm_spatial_id_origin, norm_spatial_id_destination, date, N_depart). Spatial units must have a matching ID column and geometry.
import geopandas as gpd
from adaptive_cube_plot import plot_climate_mobility_period

units = gpd.read_parquet("data/spatial/units.parquet")
fig, axes = plot_climate_mobility_period(
    ds,
    mobility="data/mobility/flows.parquet",
    spatial_units=units,
    var="METREF",
    period="2020-06-01",            # dates are grouped into days 1–15 / 16–month-end
    mobility_metric="N_depart_adj", # or N_depart / N_migrants_adj
    flow_direction="origin",        # alternatively: destination
    spatial_id_col="norm_spatial_id",
    data_crs="EPSG:4326",
    subset_type="your_subset",      # optional filter, if this column exists
    days_span=15,                    # optional filter, if this column exists
    show=False,
)
For HalfMonthIndex tables, set period_col="HalfMonthIndex" and pass the exact key as mobility_period; keep period as the climate date used for climate aggregation. Set origin_col/destination_col if your table uses other ID names. The comparison aggregates counts by origin or destination polygon; it does not draw OD flow lines. The juxtaposition is descriptive and does not establish a climate–mobility relationship. Exact temporal interpretation depends on the product timestamp semantics and the mobility period definition.



fig, ax = plot_spatial_timeseries(
    ds, var="METREF",
    points={"Site A": (-16.4, 14.5)},
    areas={"AOI": (-17.0, -16.0, 13.0, 14.0)},
    show_area_spread=True,
    show=False,
)
Point coordinates and area bounds must use the cube coordinate system. For projected data, provide projected point/bounds values; the time-series function samples the nearest grid cell and does not transform coordinates.




Automatic extent assumes rectilinear 1-D x/y coordinates; curvilinear grids need preprocessing or a dedicated plotting path.
Coastline/border detail is cartographic context, not a replacement for authoritative local boundaries.
For plain Matplotlib axes without Cartopy, a rough local aspect correction for lon/lat data is ax.set_aspect(1 / np.cos(np.deg2rad(mean_lat))); for regional maps the module uses a local projection instead. Avoid applying this correction to already-projected axes.
The automatically selected Lambert Conformal projection is intended for regional maps; choose a suitable projection explicitly for broad or unusual extents.
Mobility IDs must match the spatial-unit IDs and be consistently typed. Unmatched units appear without a mobility value.
Mobility aggregates depend on filters, adjustment factors and period semantics; inspect those before interpreting the maps.

text:
From the repository root:
from code.plot_utils.adaptive_cube_plot import (
    plot_time_slices,
    plot_spatial_timeseries,
    plot_climate_mobility_period,
)
If code is not a Python package in the local checkout, add its parent directory to sys.path, or add code/plot_utils directly:
import sys
from pathlib import Path
sys.path.insert(0, str(Path.cwd() / "code" / "plot_utils"))
from adaptive_cube_plot import plot_time_slices

title: Adaptive cube plotting
text:
import xarray as xr
from adaptive_cube_plot import plot_time_slices

ds = xr.open_zarr("data/zarr/metref_sample_1month.zarr")
fig, axes = plot_time_slices(
    ds,
    var="METREF",
    time_index=[0, 5, 10],
    data_crs="EPSG:4326",
    ncols=3,
    show=False,
)
The map extent is calculated from the selected coordinates. Set extent=(xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax) to crop all panels to a common area. data_crs describes the existing coordinate values; it does not reproject the data. Longitude/latitude coordinate names imply EPSG:4326. For projected x/y, pass the actual CRS (for example, data_crs="EPSG:32628"). Regional geographic maps default to a local Lambert Conformal projection to avoid the visual x-axis stretch of plotting longitude and latitude as equal Cartesian units. Pass a Cartopy CRS as map_crs to override it.
Overlay an AOI or administrative boundary:
import geopandas as gpd
boundaries = gpd.read_file("data/aoi.geojson")
fig, axes = plot_time_slices(
    ds, var="METREF", time_index=[0, 5], data_crs="EPSG:4326",
    boundaries=boundaries, ncols=2, show=False,
)
If a boundary file has no embedded CRS, provide boundary_crs. This assigns the source CRS metadata. Confirm the source CRS before assigning it.

title: Adaptive cube plotting
text:
The mobility table is expected to contain an origin or destination ID, a date/period column, and a numeric metric. Defaults match the normalized OD schema (norm_spatial_id_origin, norm_spatial_id_destination, date, N_depart). Spatial units must have a matching ID column and geometry.
import geopandas as gpd
from adaptive_cube_plot import plot_climate_mobility_period

units = gpd.read_parquet("data/spatial/units.parquet")
fig, axes = plot_climate_mobility_period(
    ds,
    mobility="data/mobility/flows.parquet",
    spatial_units=units,
    var="METREF",
    period="2020-06-01",            # dates are grouped into days 1–15 / 16–month-end
    mobility_metric="N_depart_adj", # or N_depart / N_migrants_adj
    flow_direction="origin",        # alternatively: destination
    spatial_id_col="norm_spatial_id",
    data_crs="EPSG:4326",
    subset_type="your_subset",      # optional filter, if this column exists
    days_span=15,                    # optional filter, if this column exists
    show=False,
)
For HalfMonthIndex tables, set period_col="HalfMonthIndex" and pass the exact key as mobility_period; keep period as the climate date used for climate aggregation. Set origin_col/destination_col if your table uses other ID names. The comparison aggregates counts by origin or destination polygon; it does not draw OD flow lines. The juxtaposition is descriptive and does not establish a climate–mobility relationship. Exact temporal interpretation depends on the product timestamp semantics and the mobility period definition.

title: Adaptive cube plotting
text:
fig, ax = plot_spatial_timeseries(
    ds, var="METREF",
    points={"Site A": (-16.4, 14.5)},
    areas={"AOI": (-17.0, -16.0, 13.0, 14.0)},
    show_area_spread=True,
    show=False,
)
Point coordinates and area bounds must use the cube coordinate system. For projected data, provide projected point/bounds values; the time-series function samples the nearest grid cell and does not transform coordinates.

title: Adaptive cube plotting
text:
Automatic extent assumes rectilinear 1-D x/y coordinates; curvilinear grids need preprocessing or a dedicated plotting path.
Coastline/border detail is cartographic context, not a replacement for authoritative local boundaries.
For plain Matplotlib axes without Cartopy, a rough local aspect correction for lon/lat data is ax.set_aspect(1 / np.cos(np.deg2rad(mean_lat))); for regional maps the module uses a local projection instead. Avoid applying this correction to already-projected axes.
The automatically selected Lambert Conformal projection is intended for regional maps; choose a suitable projection explicitly for broad or unusual extents.
Mobility IDs must match the spatial-unit IDs and be consistently typed. Unmatched units appear without a mobility value.
Mobility aggregates depend on filters, adjustment factors and period semantics; inspect those before interpreting the maps.

title: B. Download and preprocess a sample
text: This page downloads one LSA SAF product sample, crops it to a configured study area, and remaps it to a target grid. Begin with one product and one short time period. Validate the result before extending the period or region.

title: B. Download and preprocess a sample
section: 1. Check the product and study area
text:
1. Check the product and study area
The example defaults to METREF. The repository also lists FVC/MDFVC as an example product. Select a product from the LSA SAF Data Service and confirm its product URL, time coverage, variable names, units, coordinate system, no-data values and quality flags.
Coordinates are longitude/latitude in degrees in this example. For a new AOI, store it in data/aoi/ and there is a utils/ script to convert a shapefile to a bounding box. The AOI is used to crop the raw files before remapping and using standrdized coordinates. The target grid is defined in code/preprocess_utils/grid.txt. The default is a 0.05° global grid, but you can change the resolution and bounds to suit your study area.
The remapping method is bilinear by default. Use nearest-neighbour for categorical fields and flags. The remapping method is set in code/preprocess_utils/config_resolution.yaml.

title: B. Download and preprocess a sample
text:
2. Set credentials
From the repository root:
cp code/.env.example code/.env
Edit code/.env and enter your LSA SAF credentials - See the setup guide for details. The downloader expects:
LSASAF_USERNAME=your_username
LSASAF_PASSWORD=your_password
SAMPLE_YEAR=2020
SAMPLE_MONTH=06
VARIABLE_NAME=METREF
URL=https://datalsasaf.lsasvcs.ipma.pt/PRODUCTS/MSG/METREF/NETCDF
Keep code/.env private and never commit it. The script reads this path by default when run from the repository root. If you use another path, set ENV_FILE=/path/to/.env.

title: B. Download and preprocess a sample
text:
3. Download the sample
Run from the repository root:
bash code/01_download_sample.sh
You can override the year, month, product and product URL positionally:
bash code/01_download_sample.sh 2020 06 METREF "https://datalsasaf.lsasvcs.ipma.pt/PRODUCTS/MSG/METREF/NETCDF"
The script checks the service listing and skips files already present. New files are first written as .part, then renamed after a successful download. The default raw-data layout is:
data/raw/METREF/2020/06/*.nc
Confirm that files exist and have plausible sizes. A completed download only confirms transfer success; it does not confirm that the data are scientifically valid.
crumbs: B. Download and preprocess a sample

title: B. Download and preprocess a sample
text:
4. Inspect raw NetCDF before processing
Use CDO to list metadata and summary information:
cdo -s sinfo data/raw/METREF/2020/06/example.nc
cdo -s showname data/raw/METREF/2020/06/example.nc
cdo -s showtimestamp data/raw/METREF/2020/06/example.nc
cdo -s infon data/raw/METREF/2020/06/example.nc
Replace example.nc with a real downloaded filename. Review coordinate ranges, variable names, timestamps, units, missing values and product QA information. If the raw file itself has no valid values, diagnose the download/product selection before remapping.
crumbs: B. Download and preprocess a sample

title: B. Download and preprocess a sample
text:
5. Choose variables and crop/remap
Inspect the exact variable names:
cdo -s showname data/raw/METREF/2020/06/example.nc
Set the main continuous variable, AOI file and optional QA variable names:
MAIN_VARIABLE=METREF \
QA_VARIABLES=QUALITY_FLAG,QC_FLAG \
AOI_GEOJSON=data/aoi/study_area.geojson \
bash code/02_preprocess_cdo.sh data/raw/METREF data/interim
Use exact variable names from showname; QA names are comma-separated. Omit QA_VARIABLES if no QA layers are needed. The pipeline builds one snapped AOI grid from the first raw file, then checks other inputs use the same grid. It selects and bilinearly remaps only MAIN_VARIABLE by default. QA layers are selected and processed separately with nearest-neighbour mapping, which chooses an existing code rather than averaging categories. Set MAIN_REMAP_METHOD=nearest if the primary variable is categorical.
The crop includes a one-cell margin by default to support remapping near AOI edges. Outputs are written to temporary files, checked for readability and valid main-variable cells, and renamed only when complete. QA values are preserved as data layers; this example does not interpret product-specific bit fields or automatically apply a QA mask.
PARALLEL controls independent files processed concurrently; for example:
PARALLEL=2 MAIN_VARIABLE=METREF AOI_GEOJSON=data/aoi/study_area.geojson \
  bash code/02_preprocess_cdo.sh data/raw/METREF data/interim
Start conservatively. Increase parallelism only after checking RAM, disk throughput and temporary storage.
Processed files are written beneath data/interim/<MAIN_VARIABLE>/YYYY/MM/. Check data/interim/cdo.log, then inspect an output:
cdo -s sinfo data/interim/METREF/2020/06/example_processed.nc
cdo -s infon data/interim/METREF/2020/06/example_processed.nc

text:
7. Method caveats

Regridding does not add source detail. A finer target grid interpolates the source; it does not make the measurement higher resolution.
Bilinear interpolation smooths continuous fields; nearest-neighbour preserves category labels but may look blocky.
Degree-based cell size changes with latitude.
Preserve product QA flags and document any masks, unit conversion and temporal aggregation.
Record the input product/version, AOI bounds, output grid, resolution, remapping method and software version.
